rv.q: This is, to say the least, one deep dive of a star-turn, an all-consuming (and notably all-consumed) piece of acting that reveals things in Hayes that most of his 'Will and Grace' fans will be entirely gobsmacked to discover he has in his arsenal.
Hayes unleashes a career-defining performance worthy of its own reverence.
Hayes' performance in 'Good Night, Oscar' demands to be seen.
“Good Night, Oscar” provides a vehicle for Hayes to be snappy and tragic.
The play, structured around Oscar Levant’s appearance on The Tonight Show With Jack Paar in 1958, idles in neutral for the bulk of its run time.
Good Night, Oscar is less than convincing.
That thrilling moment — without mannerisms, words, other characters or exposition — is the only time Levant and “Good Night, Oscar” come to life.
But on the evidence of the character as written, and especially as impersonated by Sean Hayes in a gloomy if accurate performance, Levant doesn’t erase the line so much as fudge it.
Good Night, Oscar is a captivating work, as hysterically funny as it is heartbreaking.
Sean Hayes is just too easy to love.
There is a perhaps overused but most apt phrase to describe what is happening on stage at the Belasco, and that is "tour de force."

Sean Hayes, up till now best known for his Emmy Award-winning performance as Jack McFarland on "Will and Grace," gives a titanic performance as humorist, raconteur and pianist Oscar Levant once called the wittiest man in America, in Doug Wright’s new play "Good Night, Oscar.
A leading man offers a performance that is one for the books. It's a satisfying evening all around.
To call Hayes’ work here “a tour-de-force” performance is accurate, while not really doing it justice.
He is incomparable, acicular as barbed wire in his humor and flooring when he shows his bravery, which is to say the wounded soul beneath the proud man.
In Good Night, Oscar, Levant is a harbinger of pop-culture, for good and ill, to come—and the demons of all kinds that have shaped it.
With a less compelling performance from its lead, Good Night, Oscar would fall flat.
Like this production, it proves that a gifted performer can lift the spirit against all odds.
Doug Wright’s book, which is about greatness, is extraordinary.
While no one can fault Sean Hayes’ comic timing, there was something histrionic about much of his performance.
Other than that it is a hodge-podge of disappointing writing and direction.
Hayes was a revelation, both in his performance and his playing.
Those easy-target jokes weren’t really funny and did cross red lines.
As presented here, though, neither the man, nor his problems, provide a prescription for theatrical wellness.

cn.t: Hayes delivers a tour-de-force performance as Oscar Levant, particularly dazzling at the piano, but critics are divided on whether Wright's biographical play justifies reviving this forgotten figure.

vs.sum: The Belasco Theatre offers stunning ambiance with its historic Tiffany lamps and stained-glass ceiling, but suffers from tight legroom typical of older venues. While sound quality is generally good, sightlines can be inconsistent, especially from side orchestra seats.

acc.note: 8 wheelchair locations in Orchestra. Induction loops for t-coil hearing aids. Infrared devices available.
